headline: Peso Falls to Record ₱62.625 per Dollar as Oil and Rate Risks Build
seoTitle: Philippine Peso Hits Record ₱62.625 per Dollar | FMB News
seoDescription: The Philippine peso closed at a record ₱62.625 to the US dollar on September 8 as a stronger dollar and higher oil prices added pressure.
deck: The Philippine peso closed at a new all-time low of ₱62.625 to the US dollar on September 8, extending a year of repeated record lows as dollar strength and higher oil prices increase pressure on the currency.
author: FMB News Desk

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: The Philippine peso weakened to a new record closing low of ₱62.625 against the US dollar on Tuesday, September 8.

GMA News reported that the currency lost 3.9 centavos from Monday's ₱62.586 close and surpassed the previous record low of ₱62.59 recorded on September 4. Philippine STAR's September 8 market data separately reflected the same ₱62.625 closing rate, while the Philippine News Agency reported the peso weakening to about ₱62.62 in the same trading session.
GMA News said the September 8 close was the peso's 23rd record-low finish of 2026.

sections.heading: Context
paragraphs: The peso has been under sustained pressure from a stronger US dollar and changing expectations for US interest rates. A currency can weaken even when domestic economic activity is not collapsing if global investors prefer dollar assets or expect US rates to remain comparatively attractive.

Higher global oil prices are another pressure point for the Philippines because the country imports much of its fuel. More expensive oil increases the number of dollars needed to pay for energy imports, adding demand for foreign currency. The September 8 peso low also came on the same day as another large domestic fuel-price increase.
Economists cited by GMA News pointed to both elevated US interest-rate expectations and higher crude prices linked to Middle East tensions as major drivers of the latest move.

sections.heading: Why this matters to Filipinos
paragraphs: A weaker peso makes dollar-priced imports more expensive in local-currency terms. The most visible effects can appear in fuel, transport, food inputs, medicines, machinery, electronics and other imported goods and services.

For households receiving remittances in US dollars, a weaker peso can increase the peso value of the same dollar amount. But that benefit can be offset if imported goods and fuel become more expensive and feed into inflation.

For businesses with dollar-denominated debt or imported inputs, the exchange rate can raise costs and complicate pricing decisions. Continued peso weakness therefore matters not only to financial markets but also to household budgets and inflation management.

sections.heading: What to watch next
paragraphs: The next key questions are whether the peso stabilizes around current levels and whether global oil prices or US rate expectations move further against emerging-market currencies.

Readers should also watch the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas' policy signals, inflation data, the country's import bill and any additional escalation in Middle East energy risks. A new record low by itself does not determine the economic outlook, but repeated record lows can add to imported inflation and financial-market uncertainty.

audit.socialCaption: The Philippine peso closed at a new record low of ₱62.625 per US dollar on September 8. Dollar strength and higher oil prices are adding pressure, with possible effects on imported goods, fuel and inflation. FMB News explains why the exchange rate matters beyond the trading floor.
verificationNotes: The exact ₱62.625 closing rate is reported by GMA News and independently reflected in Philippine STAR's September 8 forex data.
PNA independently corroborates the peso's weakening in the same September 8 trading session, reporting a rounded close of about ₱62.62.
The article attributes explanations about dollar strength, oil prices and US rates to market analysis rather than presenting them as mechanically proven causes.
The article does not claim that a weak peso automatically means the Philippine economy is contracting and notes that exchange-rate movements can be driven by global conditions.
Repository search and the September 8 article directory showed no existing FMB News article centered on the ₱62.625 peso close, so this is treated as an original report.
The hero and social crops are FMB-owned editorial graphics using the approved FMB icon and purple-violet/plum treatment and are explicitly not documentary photographs.
